items.stem: A Firestore app lets any client read and write all documents in production. What is the main problem?

options.text: Security rules are too permissive and must restrict access
options.rationale: Correct: open rules let anyone read/write data; rules must enforce per-user access.
Firestore is a document database; storing documents is its purpose.
Analytics is unrelated to the data-access problem.
Hosting serves content and is unrelated to database rules.

items.explanation: Correct: Security rules are too permissive and must restrict access.

items.stem: Which TWO are appropriate uses of Cloud Functions for Firebase? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run trusted server-side logic on a Firestore write trigger
options.rationale: Correct: functions run trusted backend logic in response to events.

options.text: Expose an HTTPS callable endpoint for the app
options.rationale: Correct: callable functions give the client a secure backend endpoint.

options.text: Store the app's primary user records instead of a database
options.rationale: Functions are compute, not storage; data belongs in Firestore/RTDB.

options.text: Hold secret API keys in client code to avoid functions
options.rationale: Secrets must stay server-side; putting them in the client leaks them.

items.explanation: Correct: Run trusted server-side logic on a Firestore write trigger, Expose an HTTPS callable endpoint for the app.

items.stem: Which Firebase service should handle user sign-in with email and Google providers?

options.rationale: Correct: Authentication manages sign-in providers and user identity.
Hosting serves static content, not sign-in.
Cloud Storage holds files, not sign-in.
